newsitem.title: USA: Cereal boxes crackle as pop art - $8,500 for a 1953 Superman?.
newsitem.headline: Cereal boxes crackle as pop art - $8,500 for a 1953 Superman?.

text.p: Would you pay $8,500 for a cereal box? That's without the cereal.

So far there have been no takers. But David Welch, a memorabilia dealer, did sell another last year for $1,500 -- a 1946 Kix cereal box with a send-away coupon for the Kix Atomic Bomb Ring. And many collectors routinely pay $10 to $20 for old empty cereal boxes which are, after all, artifacts of popular American culture.
But $8,500? Even if it's for a mint-condition, unfolded 1953 Superman Kellogg's Sugar Smacks box with a miniature comic book, the only one known to still exist?

"Other Superman items have sold for $10,000 to $20,000. I'm pricing it more as a Superman item than a cereal box," said Welch, who owns Childhood Memorabilia, a dealership in Murphysboro, Ill. (618-687-2282).

Welcome to the unlikely world of cereal box collecting, where prices are popping higher, as movers and shakers indulge their taste for food packaging designs that last just about as long as a kid's attention span.

Take a look at the supermarket shelves. Batman and Robin, Jurassic Park and motorsports champions Gary Hart and Terry Labonte add crackle to a variety of Kellogg's cereals. The Flintstones pep up Post's Fruity Pebbles and Cocoa Pebbles. Wheaties crackles with an NFL All-Pro Quarterback Collectors Box and a Jackie Robinson 50th anniversary box.
That's just what's out there now. Go back to the beginning of cerealdom and you can have a museum. Some collectors do.

"An artist did it, it made an impression on my life, it's fun to have, it decorates my home," said collector Tom Tumbusch, who publishes Tomart's Price Guide to Radio Premiums and Cereal Box Collectibles (513-294-2250).
"The designs are a reflection of society," said Duane Dimock, whose collection of 13,000 boxes is likely the world's largest. His home is a virtual archive of food packaging.

Designs were simple when cerealdom began in the 1880s with Nabisco's shredded wheat. Corn flakes were invented by chance in 1894 by the brothers John Harvey Kellogg and Will Keith Kellogg, who then formed The Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Co. in 1906 to sell the flaked cereal. An industry was born.

Two-colour boxes in the 1940s gave way to colourful designs in the 1950s, psychedelia in the 1970s and a growing array of television and film characters. Now, it's metallic foil boxes and novel cereal shapes, like arrows tied in with "Prince of Thieves," the 1991 Robin Hood movie starring Kevin Costner.

Archival material can turn up in the unlikeliest of places. An unfolded 1906 corn flakes box was found backing a picture frame. Dimock paid $70 for it in 1994. He guesses it might auction for $1,000, but wouldn't part with it anyway.
But don't think you've struck gold if say, your walls yield ancient cereal boxes used as insulation -- as was the case with a 1911 Kellogg's box.

Age doesn't always count. "It doesn't matter if it's rare, it's the demand," said Tumbusch. It's boxes from the 1940s through 1960s featuring characters from TV and radio shows that feed cross-over interest and command a premium.
A rare but plain 1910 Quaker Oats box is worth just $10. But a far more common Mary Lou Retton Wheaties box from 1984 costs about $100.

A 1970 Mr. Spock Kellogg's Sugar Honey Snacks box, released only in Britain, is worth $500 to Star Trek fans. A Beatles fan has made Dimock a $3,000 standing offer for a pair of Wheat Honey and Rice Honey "Yellow Submarine" boxes from 1969.
(For icon worshippers: Elvis has yet to endorse a cereal.)

"In the early 1980s I could buy boxes for peanuts," said Jerry Cook of Fall City, Wash. "Once the fad caught on, it brought a lot of cereal boxes out of the closet, but it also raised the price, so it's a double-edged sword."
But it's still breakfast time in the cereal box market. Collectors believe there are only a few hundred of them in the United States, but the number is growing.

So budding hobbyists, if graphic design thrills you, cereal boxes can also fill you. The supermarket is the cheapest supplier. Make sure you eat the cereal first, before the bugs eat the box. And to save the most pristine box possible, open very C-A-R-E-F-U-L-L-Y.

If you catch the bug and are haunted by that Post box of breakfasts past, you can't be a Scrooge. Expect to pay $20 to $30 for a "one-shot" Barbie or other boxes as recent as circa 1990. Add a 50 percent premium for a never-folded box from the cereal company, printer or advertiser.

Pay less if the top or bottom flaps are missing. Scour flea markets and garage sales for bargains. Be financially fortified or just say "no" at shows for toys or print collectibles -- dealers are cashing in on the growing demand.
Be ready to breakfast on grits for a while if you must compete with cross-over collectors for that $8,500 Superman box or $3,000 Yellow Submarine duo.
Above all, enjoy your boxes. After all, prices can drop from their current pop. This is art to be savored even if the market loses its flavor.
